per-taedet , taesum est, 2 (quidam pertisum volunt:
I. “quod consuetudo non probavit,” Cic. Or. 48, 159 ; cf. Fest. pp. 216 sq.; 273, 8 Müll.; also Paul. ex Fest. p. 72, 18 Müll.), v. impers. and n., to be disgusted or wearied with any thing; to feel disgust at, be sick of.
(a). With gen.: “me sermonis pertaesum est,” Plaut. Most. 1, 4, 4 : “quem pertaesum est esse domi,” Lucr. 3, 1061 : “pertaesum est enim (me) levitatis,” Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 4 : “pertaesum est vos injuriae,” Sall. H. 3, 61, 8 Dietsch: “negotii,” Nep. Att. 15, 2 : “duas uxores habuerat, quarum matrimonii pertaedebat,” Gell. 15, 20, 6 : “lentitudinis eorum pertaesa,” Tac. A. 15, 51 .—
(b). With dat.: usque adeo pertaesum vos mihi esse, Gracch. ap. Diom. p. 291 P.—
(g). With acc.: “pertaesus ignaviam suam,” Suet. Caes. 7 : “pertaesus morum perversitatem ejus,” id. Aug. 62 ; id. Tib. 67.
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
